newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Profit upside, asset sales seen for Mayne.
newsitem.headline: Profit upside, asset sales seen for Mayne.

text.p: Credit rating agency Standard and Poor's Corp on Tuesday said annual profit for Australian logistics, security and health care group Mayne Nickless Ltd could exceed market forecasts.
S&P also said it expected Mayne to sell some European logistics operations soon and use the proceeds to retire debt.
"We think there's some upside in their full-year results (for the year ending June 30) from where we had been forecasting earlier," S&P analyst Duncan Warwick-Champion told Reuters.
"Probably, Mayne do have some potential upside on where people may be thinking that they are coming in," he added.
S&P declined to give their own profit forecast, but a recent survey by Barceps forecasting service shows the share market expects, on average, a profit before abnormals of A$103 million.
S&P recently considered its view on Mayne after the company last week announced it was now unclear when it could sell a major non-core investment said to be worth about A$1 billion.
Interest on funds used to finance the investment, a 25 percent stake in Australian telecom Optus Communications Pty Ltd, has begun to hurt Mayne.
Mayne has a net debt to equity ratio of over 100 percent and it had assured S&P and ratings agency Moody's Investors Service it would sell the stake by its June 30 balance date.
S&P rates Mayne "A" for long-term domestic-currency debt with a stable outlook, but says the company's interest-coverage ratios look "a little bit shy".
"We have had a look at the numbers and a bit of a discussion and we think there's still enough positives in the pipeline for Mayne," Warwick-Champion said.
"There are potential (asset) sales which we are confident that's going through of some of their surplus European logistics operations," he said.
"And we have had another look at their forecasts and Mayne have a potential upside on their revenue numbers..."
"We think there's probably enough there to keep them in the rating categaory they are currently in," he added.
S&P declined to name the offshore logistics assets up for sale, nor the likely proceeds. But a brokerage analyst said a figure of around A$250 million had been mentioned in the market.

"The market is coming to the realisation that getting rid of Optus may be a bit further down the track and therefore the only way Mayne is really going to keep things together is to drive some cash from somewhere," the analyst said.
"Asset sales are really the only other option."

Mayne said early this year it would review its investment in the European logistics business but made no further comment on Tuesday. "At this stage we have no comments on the timing of any action," spokeswoman Maryrose Winfield said.
Mayne aims to sell its Optus stake when the company is floated on the share market, but S&P believes such a float could be delayed into the second half of calendar 1998.
It was originally scheduled to take place in late 1996.
The Optus public offering may have to wait until investors have digested the one-third sale of market giant Telstra Corp. State-owned Telstra is valued at around A$30 billion.

"If they can't get in substantially before the Telstra float, which is starting to look less likely, they will have to delay themselves six to nine months, at a minimum, from the time Telstra actually floats," S&P's Warwick-Champion said.
-- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1421
